title: Double negatives and nonstandard forms
blurb: Spot double negatives (including hidden ones like hardly), nonstandard forms such as could of and irregardless, and the a/an choice.
question: A volunteer's incident note reads, “Irregardless of the sign, the visitor couldn't hardly walk, and we could of helped him sooner if them doors had been open.” How many nonstandard forms are there, and what is the standard version?

teach.body: Formally, standard English is the variety of English used in formal writing, such as textbooks, patient leaflets and test items; nonstandard forms are words or patterns common in casual speech or some dialects but not accepted in formal writing. Plain English: the HESI A2 is not judging how anyone talks. It asks which sentence would pass in a formal clinic report. Double negatives, could of, irregardless and them books all fail that test.

teach.caption: One negative per idea. Hardly, scarcely and barely already mean “almost not,” so they never pair with not, n't or no.

steps.label: Count the negatives
steps.sub: not, n't, no, none, nobody, hardly, scarcely, barely

teach.caption: Swap the second negative for its neutral partner: no → any, nobody → anybody, none → any.

head: Nonstandard
Standard
Why
rows: could of, should of, would of

teach.body: In speech, “could've” sounds exactly like “could of.” The written form must show the real word: could have, should have, would have, might have, must have. Test it by expanding the contraction: “could've” becomes “could have,” never “could of.” The same helper rule applies after any modal: “could had” and “could has” are wrong too, because modals are followed by the base form (have).

teach.h: A or an: listen, do not look

rows.label: Abbreviations
values: an MRI, an X-ray, an RN

teach.caption: Uniform starts with a “you” sound and one-time with a “w” sound, so they take a. MRI starts with “em,” so it takes an.

teach.h: Scenario: Jasmine edits an incident note
teach.body: Volunteer and nursing applicant Jasmine Ortiz reviews: “Irregardless of the sign, the visitor couldn't hardly walk, and we could of helped him sooner if them doors had been open.” Fix 1: “Regardless of the sign.” Fix 2: “could hardly walk” (hardly is already negative). Fix 3: “could have helped.” Fix 4: “if those doors had been open.” Four nonstandard forms, four one-word fixes.

teach.text: The HESI A2 keys only clear errors. Some informal-sounding forms are actually accepted in US English and will not be the tested error: “I feel badly,” “try and,” “most unique,” “drive slow,” and “less than 10 miles.” Do not pick them as the mistake when a true nonstandard form (could of, can't hardly, irregardless) is in another option.

items: One negative per idea: don't have any, can hardly, didn't see anybody.
Hardly, scarcely and barely are negative already.
Could have, should have, would have; never “of” after a helper.
Regardless, a lot, used to, supposed to, those forms, himself, themselves.
A or an by sound: an hour, an MRI, a uniform, a one-time fee.

summary: You can now find and fix double negatives, including hidden ones with hardly, scarcely and barely, and replace nonstandard forms such as could of, irregardless, alot and them books. You can also choose a or an by the first sound of the next word.

A.q: Which sentence avoids a double negative?
options: The patient can't hardly sleep because of the noise.
The patient doesn't have no appetite this morning.
The patient can barely sleep because of the noise.
The patient couldn't scarcely eat any of his dinner.
A.why: “Barely” is the only negative word, so the sentence is standard.

whyNot.0: “Can't” and “hardly” are both negative; use “can hardly.”
whyNot.1: “Doesn't” and “no” are both negative; use “doesn't have any.”
whyNot.3: “Couldn't” and “scarcely” are both negative; use “could scarcely.”

A.q: Which verb phrase correctly completes the sentence? “If we had left earlier, we ___ the bus to the testing center.”
options: could of caught
could have caught
could had caught
could've of caught
A.why: After the helper “could,” use the base form “have” plus the past participle: “could have caught.”

whyNot.0: “Of” is not a verb; “could of” is a mishearing of “could've.”
whyNot.2: “Could” is followed by the base form “have,” not “had.”
whyNot.3: “Could've” already contains “have,” so adding “of” is a second error.

A.q: Which sentence uses the articles “a” and “an” correctly?
options: The aide ordered an uniform and a hourly report.
The aide ordered a uniform and an hourly report.
The aide ordered a uniform and a hourly report.
The aide ordered an uniform and an hourly report.
A.why: “Uniform” begins with a “you” consonant sound (a uniform); “hourly” begins with a vowel sound because the h is silent (an hourly report).

whyNot.0: Both are reversed: “a uniform” and “an hourly report.”
whyNot.2: The h in “hourly” is silent, so it needs “an.”
whyNot.3: “Uniform” starts with a consonant “y” sound, so it needs “a.”

B.q: Which word or phrase correctly completes the sentence? “___ of the weather, the blood drive will open at 9 a.m.”
options: Irregardless
Regardless
Disregarding
Irregarding
B.why: “Regardless of” means without being affected by; it is the standard form.

whyNot.0: “Irregardless” doubles the negative (ir- and -less) and is nonstandard.
whyNot.2: “Disregarding” means ignoring on purpose, which does not fit a schedule that simply goes ahead.

B.q: Which sentence is written in standard English?
options: Them charts need to be signed before noon.
The surgeon finished the notes by himself.
The interns fixed the error theirselves.
This here form goes to the front desk.
B.why: “Himself” is the standard reflexive form, and it refers back to “the surgeon.”

whyNot.0: “Them” cannot point to a noun; use “Those charts.”
whyNot.3: “This here” adds an unneeded “here”; use “This form.”

B.q: Which revision corrects “Nobody didn't call the pharmacy about the refill”?
options: Nobody hasn't called the pharmacy about the refill.
Nobody called the pharmacy about the refill.
Nobody called the pharmacy about no refill.
Not nobody called the pharmacy about the refill.
B.why: “Nobody” is already negative, so the verb stays positive: “Nobody called.”

whyNot.2: “Nobody” and “no” are two negatives in the same idea.

C.q: Which word or phrase correctly completes the sentence? “The clinic ___ open at 6 a.m. before the new schedule began.”
options: use to
used to
useta
uses to
C.why: The past-habit form is “used to,” with the -d written even though it is hard to hear.

whyNot.0: Without “did” before it, the written form needs the -d: “used to.”
whyNot.2: “Useta” spells out casual speech and is not standard written English.
whyNot.3: “Uses to” is not a standard form for a past habit.

C.q: Which sentence contains a double negative?
options: The aide hardly had time to chart before the next admission.
There wasn't any reason to delay the discharge paperwork.
The patient hadn't barely finished lunch when the doctor came.
None of the visitors brought food into the isolation room.
C.why: “Hadn't” and “barely” are both negatives; the standard form is “had barely finished.”

whyNot.0: “Hardly” is the only negative word in the sentence.
whyNot.1: “Wasn't” is the only negative; “any” is neutral.
whyNot.3: “None” is the only negative word in the sentence.

C.q: Which word or phrase correctly completes the sentence? “Being a new graduate, Jalen learned ___ during his first week on the unit.”
options: alot
a lot
allot
a lots
C.why: “A lot” (a great deal) is always written as two words.

whyNot.0: “Alot” is not standard English; write “a lot.”
whyNot.2: “Allot” is a verb meaning to give out shares, which does not fit after “learned.”

reteach.title: Two minus signs
reteach.question: In math, two minus signs can cancel each other out. Why does the same thing make “I don't have no gloves” confusing in a formal report?

blocks.body: Formal English treats a negative like a minus sign. “I don't have any gloves” has one minus sign and means zero gloves. “I don't have no gloves” stacks two, and a strict reader could take it as “I do have gloves.” Hidden minus signs count too: hardly, scarcely and barely each carry one. Keep one minus sign per idea and the meaning stays exact, which is what a clinic note needs.

blocks.h: Swap the second minus for a neutral word
head: Two minus signs
One minus sign

blocks.text: “I couldn't care less” is standard: it means you could not possibly care less. It has one negative, not two.

explain.body: Use one negative per idea. Replace the second negative with its neutral partner: no → any, nobody → anybody, none → any.

test.q: Which sentence is written in standard English with no double negative?
options: There isn't no reason to skip the follow-up visit.
The pharmacy didn't have any of the brand-name tablets.
The nurse didn't see nobody in the waiting room.
We don't need none of the extra forms today.
test.why: “Didn't” is the only negative; “any” is neutral.

whyNot.0: “Isn't” and “no” are two negatives; use “There is no reason.”
whyNot.2: “Didn't” and “nobody” are two negatives; use “didn't see anybody.”
whyNot.3: “Don't” and “none” are two negatives; use “don't need any.”

explain.body: Hardly, scarcely and barely mean “almost not.” They are negative already, so they never pair with not or n't.

test.q: Which phrase correctly completes the sentence? “After the injection, Mr. Ruiz ___ lift his arm above his shoulder.”
options: couldn't hardly
could hardly
couldn't barely
couldn't scarcely
test.why: “Hardly” is already negative, so the helper stays positive: “could hardly.”

explain.body: Could, should, would, might and must are followed by the base form “have” plus a past participle. “Of” only sounds like “’ve.”

test.q: Which revision corrects the verb error in “You should of called the clinic before you drove over”?
options: Change “should of called” to “should have called.”
Change “should of called” to “should had called.”
Change “should of called” to “should of call.”
Change “drove” to “had drove.”
test.why: After “should,” use “have” plus the past participle: “should have called.”

whyNot.1: “Should” is followed by the base form “have,” not “had.”
whyNot.2: Changing the participle leaves the nonstandard “of” in place.
whyNot.3: “Drove” is correct, and “had drove” adds an error (had driven).

explain.body: Choose by the first SOUND of the next word, not its first letter. Silent h and vowel-sounding abbreviations take an; a long-u “you” sound and a “w” sound take a.

test.q: Which phrase uses the correct article?
options: a honest answer
an X-ray order
an one-time fee
an urinalysis kit
test.why: “X-ray” is read “ex-ray,” starting with a vowel sound, so it takes “an.”

whyNot.0: The h in “honest” is silent, so it takes “an”: an honest answer.
whyNot.2: “One-time” starts with a “w” sound, so it takes “a.”
whyNot.3: “Urinalysis” starts with a “you” sound, so it takes “a.”
